title: AI Glossary
note: Terms follow the Stanford HAI glossary; definitions are short paraphrased summaries. See the source for the full official wording.

terms.definition: An attack where someone covertly tampers with a model's training process, typically while a smaller model is being trained to copy a larger one.
A hypothetical AI with human-level or greater ability to learn, reason and apply knowledge across many different tasks and fields.
AI that works as an autonomous or semi-autonomous agent: it interprets goals, plans steps, uses tools such as browsers, code or APIs, reacts to feedback and adapts to finish tasks.
Ensuring an AI system's goals and behaviour match human values, rules and intentions.
Standardised tests used to measure and compare AI performance on tasks like question answering, image recognition, coding or instruction following.
The ability to work productively and responsibly with AI: knowing its strengths and limits, judging its outputs critically, using it ethically and keeping up as it changes.
The field focused on making AI systems reliable and harmless, even when powerful, widely deployed or facing unexpected situations.
The combined software, hardware and compute that supports the whole AI lifecycle, from data through training to deployment.
The end-to-end process of building, deploying and maintaining an AI system: data preparation, training, testing and deployment, each stage feeding the next.
A step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, much like a recipe.
When many organisations rely on the same or very similar AI models, algorithms or training data.
A network of AI systems or agents that share information and coordinate their actions as a collective.
The science and engineering of building intelligent machines; the term was coined in 1955 by John McCarthy, Stanford's first AI faculty member.
A neural-network technique that lets a model weigh and focus on the most relevant parts of its input when producing output.
Technology, including AI, carrying out specific tasks according to explicit, predefined human instructions.
The method neural networks use to learn from errors by working backward through the layers to find which weights contributed to a mistake and adjusting them.
Graphical models that use probabilities to represent how variables influence one another, like a map of cause and effect.
When an AI system produces outcomes that unfairly favour or disadvantage certain groups of people.
Datasets too large for traditional processing tools, which AI can analyse to uncover patterns and trends.
A program that simulates conversation with people through text or voice.
Proprietary software whose code is not publicly available to view, modify or reuse.
The AI field that lets computers interpret and understand images and video, similar to human sight.
The maximum amount of input, such as text, a model can take into account at one time.
A training approach where a model learns by comparing similar and dissimilar examples to understand what makes things alike or different.
Expanding a training set by creating modified copies of existing data (e.g. rotated or cropped images) rather than collecting new data.
Using statistics and machine learning to discover patterns and trends in large datasets.
An attack that deliberately inserts, alters or mislabels training data to corrupt how a model behaves.
A model that predicts by asking a series of yes/no questions about features, splitting the data at each step until reaching an answer.
A branch of machine learning that uses large, many-layered neural networks to learn complex patterns automatically from data.
Generative models that learn to create content such as images by adding noise to data and then learning to remove it step by step.
Simplifying data by cutting down the number of variables while keeping the most important information.
Numeric vectors that represent words, images or other objects in a way that captures their meaning or characteristics.
Techniques that combine several models (often weak learners) to get predictions more accurate and robust than any single model.
Designing, building and deploying AI in line with human values, fairness, transparency and social well-being.
Rule-based programs that imitate a human expert's decisions in a narrow domain using a knowledge base and if-then rules.
Methods that make an AI system's decisions understandable to humans instead of leaving it an opaque black box.
Training a shared model across many devices or servers that keep their data locally, so raw data never leaves its source.
Getting a model to learn a new task or category from only a handful of examples.
Further training a pre-trained model on task- or domain-specific data to specialise it.
Large models, often transformers, trained on broad and diverse data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks.
A highly capable general-purpose model at or near the cutting edge of AI development.
AI that creates new content such as text, images, music, code or video.
An architecture where a generator network and a discriminator network compete, pushing the generator to produce realistic synthetic data.
A family of large language models built on the transformer architecture that generate human-like text from prompts.
A chip originally built for rendering graphics that performs many calculations in parallel, making it well suited to training and running AI.
When an AI system produces incorrect, misleading or made-up information while presenting it as fact.
An approach to AI that puts human needs, values and well-being first throughout development and deployment.
How people operate and engage with computer systems, and the study of designing those interactions.
AI systems that build human feedback or intervention into their operation.
A setting chosen before training starts (like learning rate or number of layers) rather than learned from data.
A large tech company running vast data-center networks that can quickly scale compute, storage and cloud services.
When a trained model makes predictions or decisions on new, unseen data.
How well humans can understand the way an AI system reaches its decisions or predictions.
A simple algorithm for classification and regression that predicts based on the k most similar examples in the data.
Training a smaller 'student' model to imitate the outputs and behaviour of a larger 'teacher' model.
A structured database that stores information as a network of entities and the relationships between them.
An AI system trained on huge amounts of text to understand and generate human-like language.
A compressed, lower-dimensional mathematical space where data like images or text is encoded to capture its essential features.
Practices for managing the full lifecycle of LLM-based applications in production.
A mathematical measure (also called cost or objective function) of how far a model's predictions are from the correct values.
A branch of AI where computers learn patterns and make decisions from data instead of following hand-written rules.
A model of a sequence of events where the chance of the next state depends only on the current state, not the full history.
Practices that merge machine learning, software engineering and DevOps to deploy, monitor and maintain ML models reliably in production.
A simplified mathematical or computational representation of a real-world system used to make predictions or find patterns.
A drop in a model's performance over time because real-world data has shifted away from the data it was trained on.
AI that can process, understand and generate several data types together, such as text, images, audio and video.
The AI field focused on enabling computers to understand, interpret and generate human language.
A brain-inspired model made of layers of interconnected artificial neurons that process and pass along information.
A method (such as gradient descent) that adjusts a model's parameters to reduce its errors.
When a model memorises its training data, including noise and errors, and so performs poorly on new data.
A model whose weights, code, training data (or a detailed auditable account of it) and tools are available for anyone to download, run, inspect, reproduce and modify.
A model whose trained weights are publicly released for download, without necessarily sharing training data or full code.
Software whose source code is made freely available for anyone to view and use.
An internal variable of a model that is learned and adjusted during training.
Using data, statistics and machine learning to forecast future outcomes or trends.
Crafting instructions (prompts) carefully to steer a language model toward the desired output.
An attack that uses malicious input to trick an LLM into ignoring its instructions or behaving in unintended ways.
A technique where a language model first retrieves relevant external, up-to-date information and then uses it to generate better answers.
An AI model built to tackle complex problems by producing a logical, step-by-step chain of thought.
Learning by trial and error, where an agent takes actions in an environment and improves based on rewards or penalties.
The frameworks, principles and practices that guide ethical and safe AI development and deployment.
The field combining engineering, computer science and increasingly AI to build machines that perform physical tasks.
The ability to understand and reason about the 3D physical world: how objects relate, move and interact in space.
Training where a model generates its own learning tasks from raw, unlabeled data (e.g. predicting hidden parts) and learns by solving them.
Working out the meaning of language by examining relationships between words, phrases and symbols.
Predictable relationships showing how model performance improves as model size, data and compute grow.
Training a model on labeled data, where each input comes paired with the correct answer.
Artificially generated data produced by algorithms or simulations instead of collected from real events.
A multi-dimensional container of numbers, like a more advanced spreadsheet, used as the basic data structure in deep learning.
Splitting text into smaller units (tokens) such as words, sub-words or characters that a language model can process.
Earlier AI approaches built on explicitly programmed rules, logic and human-defined knowledge rather than learning from data.
The examples (text, images, audio, etc.) used to teach a machine learning model to perform a task.
Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for a different but related task.
A neural-network architecture that uses attention to relate all parts of the input at once rather than in sequence; the basis of modern LLMs.
A test proposed by Alan Turing in 1950 of whether a machine's behaviour can be indistinguishable from a human's.
Training on unlabeled data so the model finds patterns and structure on its own.
A database built to store and quickly search high-dimensional vectors (embeddings) of text, images or audio.
The transformer architecture adapted from language to analysing images, typically by treating image patches like tokens.
The numeric parameters in a neural network that set the strength of connections between neurons and shape how the model processes input.
A model's ability to handle tasks or categories it was never explicitly trained on, using its general knowledge.
